capitals.name: La Centinela (Chincha Alta)
capitals.note: 'La Centinela was the Incan capital of the kingdom of the Chincha'; the Chincha page calls it 'part of what used to be the capital of the Kingdom of Chincha'. No dates on either page. La Centinela is not in the gazetteer: coordinates are those of Chincha Alta, used as a proxy.

correction.text: the Chincha valley: roughly triangular, about 25 km north to south along the coast and 20 km inland

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1000-1479: 'The Chincha culture came to dominate the whole valley'; the valley is 'about 25 km north to south along the coast and about 20 km inland'. The page also has the Chincha 'expanding up and down the coast of Peru' in the 14th and 15th centuries without a span; that growth is not drawn. [Reviewer am-04, 2026-10-19: area: the 25 km disc resolves to 5 grid cells, about 1,260 km2, against about 500 km2 for a valley 25 km by 20 km (ratio about 2.5); kept as the smallest drawable extent at the grid's resolution]

region.text: the Chincha valley: roughly triangular, about 25 km north to south along the coast and 20 km inland

ledger.note: 11th century: the Chincha culture begins. 'In the 11th century, the sophisticated and warlike culture known as the Chincha began' (a 'Pre-Chincha' culture appeared in the 9th-10th centuries; Late Intermediate Period 900-1450). The page gives no year; 1000 is the bridge.

region.text: the Chincha valley: roughly triangular, about 25 km north to south along the coast and 20 km inland

ledger.note: c. 1480: the Chincha Kingdom is annexed by the Inca. 'Part of the Inca Empire around 1480', 'a true territorial annexation' under Topa Inca Yupanqui (1471-93); the Chincha lords kept much of their autonomy and Atahualpa called the Chincha lord 'his friend'. The first Inca expedition under Capac Yupanqui in Pachacuti's reign had been an attempt at friendly relations.

region.text: the Chincha valley: roughly triangular, about 25 km north to south along the coast and 20 km inland

ledger.note: c. 1480: the independent Chincha Kingdom ends. Its lord, mistaken for Atahualpa for his display of wealth, was killed at Cajamarca in 1532; the Spanish reached the valley in 1534 and the population fell about 99% in 85 years.

wars.name: Inca annexation of the Chincha Kingdom

zones.text: the Chincha valley: roughly triangular, about 25 km north to south along the coast and 20 km inland

wars.outcome: Annexation under Topa Inca Yupanqui, around 1480; the Chincha kept much of their political and economic autonomy.
wars.note: Preceded by a first Inca expedition under Capac Yupanqui in Pachacuti's reign (undated), 'according to some sources' an attempt at friendly relations, not conquest.

certainty.note: A single valley: the page gives its size (25 km by 20 km), no frontier.

sources.title: Chincha people (Chincha Kingdom)
sources.note: Late Intermediate Period 900-1450; Chincha began in the 11th century; valley 25 km by 20 km; Inca annexation under Topa Inca Yupanqui, 'around 1480'; lord killed at Cajamarca 1532; Spanish 1534.

sources.title: List of wars involving the Inca Empire
sources.note: Dates an Inca-Chincha war 1440-1460 ('Inca victory') and a Huarco-Inca war in the 1450s.

notes: Wikipedia's article is 'Chincha people' (a search for 'Chincha Kingdom' did not load). Predecessors on the page: Paracas (from about 800 BCE), Topará, Ica-Nazca influence (100 BCE-800 CE), Wari influence or control (about 500-1000 CE); none has a dossier except Nazca/Wari, which are not linked because the page names influence only. The start year 1000 is a bridge for 'the 11th century'. The page says the Chincha controlled maritime trade (Spondylus from Ecuador, 1,400 km north) and expanded along the coast in the 14th-15th centuries without dates or limits: not drawn. Population: 30,000 households, 'more than 100,000 people under Chincha control' (undated). The Inca Empire dossier carries the matching gain at 1480. The List of wars involving the Inca Empire page dates an Inca-Chincha war 1440-1460 (Inca victory), against the Chincha page's annexation 'around 1480' under Topa Inca Yupanqui; the Chincha page's date is kept, the list's would end the kingdom twenty years earlier.
